extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical mechanics / mathematics; readers of Archimedes and historians of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Archimedes' propositions and postulates about buoyancy, equilibrium, and stability of solids in fluids (including the law of displacement, apparent weight in fluid, and stability conditions for spherical and paraboloid segments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I.5 — Equilibrium immersion equals displaced fluid weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Any solid lighter than a fluid will, if placed in the fluid, be so far immersed that the weight of the solid will be equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses geometrical constructions (pyramids with vertex at Earth's centre, equal/similar pyramids, portion of fluid equal to immersed solid) and the requirement that pressures on parts of the fluid must be equal for rest; concluding the weight of the corresponding portion of fluid equals the weight of the solid, hence equals the weight of fluid displaced by the immersed portion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I.6 — Upthrust equals difference between weight and displaced fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid lighter than a fluid be forcibly immersed in it, the solid will be driven upwards by a force equal to the difference between its weight and the weight of the fluid displaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: add to the immersed solid a lighter solid so combined body attains equilibrium with part projecting; difference between weight of combined body and weight of equal volume of fluid gives the upward force on the originally immersed body. Concludes the upward (buoyant) force equals (weight of fluid displaced) − (apparent weight difference), i.e. the difference between solid's weight and weight of displaced fluid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I.7 — Heavier solids sink; apparent loss equals displaced fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) A solid heavier than a fluid will, if placed in it, descend to the bottom of the fluid. (2) The solid, when weighed in the fluid, is lighter than its true weight by the weight of the fluid displaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Intuitive pressure argument: fluid under the solid is at greater pressure so other parts give way until it reaches bottom. (2) Proof by combining the heavy solid with a lighter solid chosen so that the combined body has same weight as an equal volume of fluid → combined body remains stationary; from this deduce that the sinking force (apparent weight loss) equals the weight of the displaced fluid. Application: outlines Archimedes' method for determining composition of a crown by comparing apparent weight losses (or displaced volumes) of known metals and the crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 2 — Direction of upward force through centre of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Let it be granted that bodies which are forced upwards in a fluid are forced upwards along the perpendicular [to the surface] which passes through their centre of gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is taken as a postulate (assumption) used in subsequent equilibrium/stability arguments to fix the line of action of the buoyant force as the perpendicular through the submerged portion's centre of gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I.8 — Spherical segment axis perpendicular when base not touching
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid in the form of a segment of a sphere, and of a substance lighter than a fluid, be immersed in it so that its base does not touch the surface, the solid will rest in such a position that its axis is perpendicular to the surface; and, if the solid be forced into such a position that its base touches the fluid on one side and be then set free, it will not remain in that position but will return to the symmetrical position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: cut by a plane through the axis and Earth's centre; compare centres of gravity of parts inside/outside fluid and use lines of action of weight and fluid pressure to show equilibrium only when axis perpendicular. Note: proof missing in Latin source; later editor Commandinus supplied a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I.9 — Spherical segment with base below surface rests axis perpendicular
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid in the form of a segment of a sphere, and of a substance lighter than a fluid, be immersed in it so that its base is completely below the surface, the solid will rest in such a position that its axis is perpendicular to the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutilated proof survives for the case where the segment is greater than a hemisphere: similar method as I.8 — consider centres of gravity of parts and show imbalance unless axis perpendicular; proofs for other cases are only fragmentary in the manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 1 — Ratio relation between weights and immersed fraction
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid lighter than a fluid be at rest in it, the weight of the solid will be to that of the same volume of the fluid as the immersed portion of the solid is to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic/geometric argument: compare the solid (A+B) and an equal volume of fluid (C+D) with decomposition so that weights and volumes relate; deduce equality of weights of certain parts and hence the proportionality between immersed fraction and weight ratio (i.e., specific gravity equals immersed fraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 2 — Paraboloid segment returns to vertical (axis ≤ 3p)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a right segment of a paraboloid of revolution whose axis is not greater than 3p (where p is the principal parameter of the generating parabola), and whose specific gravity is less than that of a fluid, be placed in the fluid with its axis inclined to the vertical at any angle, but so that the base of the segment does not touch the surface of the fluid, the segment of the paraboloid will not remain in that position but will return to the position in which its axis is vertical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometrical proof: take plane through axis perpendicular to fluid surface, intersect paraboloid in a parabola, examine tangent parallel to surface-chord, locate centres of gravity of whole and immersed portion (C and F), draw connecting line and normals; show the resultant buoyant force and weight produce a moment tending to restore axis to vertical. Some steps supplied by later editors where manuscript is deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 3 — Paraboloid segment returns to vertical when base submerged (axis ≤ 3p)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a right segment of a paraboloid of revolution whose axis is not greater than 3p, and whose specific gravity is less than that of a fluid, be placed in the fluid with its axis inclined at any angle to the vertical, but so that its base is entirely submerged, the solid will not remain in that position but will return to the position in which the axis is vertical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof parallels Prop. 2 but for the case where the base is completely submerged: construct tangent and diameter at contact point, identify centres of gravity of submerged and unsubmerged portions, and show the restoring moment acts to make axis vertical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 4 — Stability criterion for paraboloid segment (axis > 2p)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a right segment of a paraboloid of revolution whose axis AN is greater than 2p (where p is the parameter), and whose specific gravity is less than that of a fluid but bears to it a ratio not less than (AN−3p)²:AN², if the segment be placed in the fluid with its axis at any inclination to the vertical, but so that its base does not touch the surface of the fluid, it will not remain in that position but will return to the position in which its axis is vertical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a quantitative stability condition: if the specific gravity ratio meets the stated lower bound (expressed in terms of the axis length and parameter p), then the vertical axis position is stable; proof uses calculations comparing positions of centres of gravity and normals to the tangent at the immersion boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 5 — Complementary stability bound for submerged base
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a right segment of a paraboloid of revolution such that its axis AN is greater than p, and its specific gravity is less than that of a fluid but in a ratio to it not greater than {AN² − (AN−3p)²}:AN², if the segment be placed in the fluid with its axis inclined at any angle to the vertical, but so that its base is completely submerged, it will not remain in that position but will return to the position in which AN is vertical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another quantitative condition bounding the specific gravity from above (relative to the geometry) ensuring the vertical position is restoring when the base is fully submerged. Proof again uses centres of gravity, construction of perpendiculars to tangent, and inequalities derived from parabola properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 6 — No single-point contact stability (axis conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a right segment of a paraboloid lighter than a fluid be such that its axis AM is greater than 3p, but AM:4p < 15:4, and if the segment be placed in the fluid with its axis so inclined to the vertical that its base touches the fluid, it will never remain in such a position that the base touches the surface in one point only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive geometric proof: choose specific points along axis (centres of gravity), draw tangents and diameters, relate distances and show the moment about contact forces the body to turn away from the single-point touching configuration; includes algebraic inequalities and a supplement that a shorter proof exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 7 — Single-point contact impossible for submerged-base case (axis bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a right segment of a paraboloid of revolution lighter than a fluid and such that its axis AM is greater than p but AM: p < 15:4, if the segment be placed in the fluid so that its base is entirely submerged, it will never rest in such a position that the base touches the surface of the fluid at one point only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to Prop. 6 but for the case base entirely submerged; uses centre-of-gravity constructions and perpendiculars to tangents to show the single-point contact gives non-equilibrium and the body will rotate away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 8 — Existence of non-vertical equilibrium angle (AM>3p, specific gravity small)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a solid in the form of a right segment of a paraboloid of revolution whose axis AM is greater than 3p, but such that AM:3p < 15:4, and whose specific gravity bears to that of a fluid a ratio less than (AM−3p)²:AM², then, if the solid be placed in the fluid so that its base does not touch the fluid and its axis is inclined to the vertical, the solid will not return to the position in which its axis is vertical and will not remain in any position except that in which its axis makes with the surface of the fluid a certain angle to be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This asserts the possibility of a stable oblique equilibrium (a non-vertical angle of rest) when geometry and specific gravity satisfy certain inequalities. Proof divides into cases using constructed points X,Y etc., and shows restoring/preventing moments lead to a specific equilibrium angle determined by the geometry and density ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 9 — Complementary existence of oblique equilibrium (specific gravity large)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a solid in the form of a right segment of a paraboloid of revolution whose axis AM is greater than 2p, but such that AM:p < 15:4, and whose specific gravity bears to that of a fluid a ratio greater than {AM² − (AM−3p)²}:AM², then, if the solid be placed in the fluid with its axis inclined at an angle to the vertical but so that its base is entirely below the surface, the solid will not return to the position in which its axis is vertical and will not remain in any position except that in which its axis makes with the surface of the fluid an angle equal to that described in the last proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mirror statement of Prop. 8 for the opposite inequality in density: predicts an oblique equilibrium angle for the submerged-base case; proof again proceeds by comparing centres of gravity and showing the lines of action of weights and buoyant forces align only at that particular angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Proposition 10 — Classification of equilibrium positions for axis long (AM:4p > 15:4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a solid in the form of a right segment of a paraboloid of revolution in which the axis AM is of a length such that AM:4p > 15:4, and supposing the solid placed in a fluid of greater specific gravity so that its base is entirely above the surface, to investigate the positions of rest. The enunciation gives a full classification (I–V) of possible rest positions depending on the ratio (specific gravity of solid):(specific gravity of fluid) compared with several critical ratios (AR²:AM², QQ₂:AM², P,P:AM² etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary of cases given: (I) if density ratio ≤ AR²:AM² (i.e. ≤ (AM−2p):AM²?) the solid rests vertical (stable); (II) if between AR²:AM² and QQ₂:AM² then it does not rest with single-point contact but rests with axis at an angle greater than a threshold; (IIIa) if equal to QQ₂:AM² there is equilibrium with single-point contact at a specified angle; (IIIb) another equality gives single-point contact at a different angle; (IV) if density ratio greater than P,P:AM², the solid rests with its base more submerged; (V) if density ratio less than P,P:AM² the solid rests with axis inclined less than threshold but base not touching. The proposition's proof is long and constructive: it builds similar parabolic segments, uses many centre-of-gravity constructions, tangent/subnormal properties, and derives the inequalities that determine which of these equilibrium types occurs.
